name: Adding Lightness
price: Free to register, about $11 a year
story: Colin Chapman, the founder of Lotus, had one rule for building race cars: simplify, then add lightness. You cannot add lightness, and yet his cars won seven Formula 1 constructors' titles with less power than their rivals. It is the Bending Spoons kind of name, an impossible act, and it is also the whole product philosophy in two words: every good thing you ship is something you took away.

name: Signed Inside
price: Free to register, about $11 a year
story: In 1982 the team that built the first Macintosh signed a sheet of paper. Steve Jobs had the signatures moulded into the inside of every case, where no customer would ever look, because real artists sign their work. A name for a company that puts its name on everything it ships, even the parts nobody opens.

name: Eight Proofs
price: Free to register, about $11 a year
story: Gauss called one result his golden theorem. He proved it at 19. Then he proved it again, and again, eight different ways across his life, because no single proof satisfied him. One right answer is enough for most people. Eight is taste. A number plus a noun, like 37signals, for founders who came out of a maths school.

name: Crown Flint
price: Free to register, about $11 a year
story: Every good lens is two pieces of glass: one of crown glass, one of flint glass. Each bends colour wrongly on its own. Put together, they cancel each other's error and the image comes out sharp. That is how telescopes and cameras became possible. A name about co-founders, and about products where two imperfect parts make one clear thing.

name: Vine Black
price: Free to register, about $11 a year
story: One of the oldest blacks in painting is vine black: charred grapevine twigs, ground to powder. Painters have used it since antiquity and it does not fade. A deep, lasting thing made out of almost nothing. Short, dark and elegant, and it already looks good on a black hoodie.

name: Forty Flags
price: Free to register, about $11 a year
story: The International Code of Signals is exactly forty flags. With them, any ship can talk to any other ship, in any language, anywhere on the sea. It is the closest cousin of 37signals there is: a number, a noun, and a story about a small set of simple things that lets the whole world connect. 40flags.com is free too.

name: Painting Air
price: Free to register, about $11 a year
story: Claude Monet, 1895: other painters paint a bridge, a house, a boat. I want to paint the air in which the bridge, the house and the boat are, and that is nothing less than the impossible. The same shape as Bending Spoons. For a company that cares about the part of a product nobody can point at: the feel.

name: Venus Arc
price: Free to register, about $11 a year
story: On 6 June 1761, in St Petersburg, Mikhail Lomonosov watched Venus cross the Sun. Everyone saw the same thing. He alone noticed a hair-thin arc of light around the planet and concluded, correctly and first, that Venus has an atmosphere. A name about seeing what everybody looked at and nobody saw.

name: Dash Eighty
price: Free to register, about $11 a year
story: In 1955 Boeing had one prototype jet, the Dash 80, and every airline boss in America watching from the shore. Test pilot Tex Johnston flew it over them and rolled it upside down. Asked what he thought he was doing, he said: I was selling airplanes. The plane became the 707. A name for people who show the product instead of the deck.

name: Dazzle Fleet
price: Free to register, about $11 a year
story: In 1917 the Royal Navy could not hide its ships from submarines. So the painter Norman Wilkinson did the opposite: thousands of ships were painted in loud cubist stripes, so no periscope could tell which way they were going. Design as a weapon, and the bravest brief a designer ever got. The best sounding name on the list.
